questions.question: Using the key figures from the lesson, explain why South Africa is described as a water-scarce country, referring to rainfall amount, distribution, seasonality, evaporation and runoff.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa's average annual rainfall is about 465 millimetres against a world average of about 860 — barely more than half. The rain is unevenly distributed in space, decreasing from east to west: parts of the KwaZulu-Natal coast and eastern escarpment receive more than 1 000 millimetres, the central plateau 400 to 600, and the west under 200, with the coastal strip near the Orange mouth under 50; roughly two thirds of the country receives less than the 500 millimetres conventionally needed for rain-fed crop farming. The rain is also uneven in time: most regions have summer rainfall, the south-western Cape winter rainfall, and only a thin southern coastal strip year-round rain, while totals swing widely between drought and flood years, with the largest percentage swings in the driest areas. Evaporation compounds the scarcity: over most of the interior, potential evaporation exceeds annual rainfall — above 2 500 millimetres in parts of the Northern Cape — so open water constantly steams back into the sky. The result is that only about 9 per cent of rainfall ever reaches the rivers as runoff, and most of that economically capturable runoff has already been allocated, placing South Africa among the thirty driest countries on earth.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's major rivers and classify river types, explaining how the pattern of perennial, periodic and episodic rivers relates to the rainfall map, and why South Africa has almost no natural lakes.
questions.expected_answer: The Orange or Gariep, the country's great river, rises in the Lesotho highlands where rain and snow are heaviest, and flows about 2 200 kilometres westward to the Atlantic at Alexander Bay, staying perennial across near-desert because it carries Lesotho's mountain water; its major tributary, the Vaal, drains the industrial heartland and supplies Gauteng, which sits on a watershed plateau with no major river of its own. Eastward to the Indian Ocean flow short, steep but strong rivers draining the wet escarpment slopes — the Thukela, whose water is pumped into the Vaal system, plus the Limpopo, Komati and Pongola; the south has the Breede and Gouritz, and the winter-rainfall south-west the Berg and the Western Cape Olifants. Perennial rivers flow all year and rise in the high-rainfall east and south; periodic rivers flow only in and after the rainy season in the middle country; episodic rivers, such as the Molopo and Auob of the Karoo and Kalahari, flow only occasionally after rare storms and may lie dry for years. Moving west, river types change in exactly the order the declining rainfall predicts. South Africa has almost no natural lakes — exceptions include landslide-dammed Lake Fundudzi, the Chrissiesmeer pans and coastal Sibaya — because natural lakes require glacial scouring or surplus river water, and the dry, warm climate provided neither; the country therefore built more than 500 large dams instead.

questions.question: Discuss the physical and human factors that influence the availability of water in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Physical factors: rainfall amount sets the ceiling at about 465 millimetres against the world's 860; distribution places the water in the east while the west receives little; seasonality and variability deliver water in bursts, in one season, in some years, making storage essential; evaporation exceeds rainfall over most of the interior, shrinking every dam and pan; relief and geology decide dam sites and aquifer storage — the escarpment gives short, steep eastern rivers, while dolomite in the North West and Gauteng holds strong aquifers; and the low runoff ratio of about 9 per cent compresses modest rain into very little river. Human factors: the population and economic map is mismatched with the water map — Gauteng concentrates people and industry on a riverless plateau, so water must be transferred to it; demand grows with population, urbanisation and industrialisation, with irrigation agriculture the largest user at around 60 per cent; pollution removes water from use — failing sewage works, industrial effluent, fertiliser runoff feeding algal blooms and acid mine drainage from old Witwatersrand workings; alien invasive plants such as wattles, pines and gums consume measurably more water along watercourses than indigenous vegetation; infrastructure losses see more than a third of municipal water leak or go unbilled in many towns; and management itself matters, because in a dry country availability is made, not found — through storage, transfer, treatment, maintenance and law.
